title: Series Resonance Circuit
short_intro: A series L-C-R circuit exhibits resonance when the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance at a specific driving frequency. At this resonant frequency, the impedance of the circuit is purely resistive and attains its minimum value, resulting in maximum current flow.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding the condition for resonance, calculation of resonant frequency, impedance, phase angle, and maximum current in a series L-C-R circuit connected to an AC source.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Advanced analysis involving Quality factor (Q-factor), bandwidth, sharpness of resonance, selectivity, and frequency response curves under varying circuit parameters.

prerequisites: Alternating current fundamentals and phasor representation
Reactance of inductors and capacitors (X<sub>L</sub> and X<sub>C</sub>)

concept_notes.heading: Condition for Series Resonance
bullets: Resonance occurs in a series L-C-R circuit when the inductive reactance X<sub>L</sub> is equal to the capacitive reactance X<sub>C</sub>.
Mathematically, this condition is expressed as ωL = 1/(ωC), where ω is the angular frequency of the AC source, L is inductance, and C is capacitance.
Under this condition, the net reactance of the circuit (X<sub>L</sub> - X<sub>C</sub>) becomes zero.

concept_notes.heading: Impedance and Phase at Resonance
bullets: The total impedance of a series L-C-R circuit is given by Z = √[R<sup>2</sup> + (X<sub>L</sub> - X<sub>C</sub>)<sup>2</sup>].
At resonance, since X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>, the impedance Z reaches its minimum possible value, which is equal to the pure resistance R.
The phase angle φ between the alternating voltage and current becomes zero, meaning the voltage and current are in phase, and the power factor is unity (cosφ = 1).

concept_notes.heading: Current and Voltage Magnification
bullets: Because the impedance is minimum (Z = R), the RMS current in the circuit reaches its maximum value: I<sub>max</sub> = V/R.
At resonance, the potential drop across the inductor and capacitor can be much larger than the applied source voltage, a phenomenon known as voltage magnification.
The voltage across the inductor (or capacitor) at resonance is Q times the applied source voltage, where Q is the quality factor.

concept_notes.heading: Quality Factor (Q-factor) and Selectivity
bullets: The Q-factor of a series resonant circuit is a measure of the sharpness of resonance or the selectivity of the circuit.
It is defined as the ratio of the potential drop across either the inductor or capacitor to the applied voltage at resonance.
Higher values of L/R or lower values of R sharpen the resonance curve, narrowing the bandwidth (Δω = R/L).

derivations.title: Derivation of Resonant Frequency
derivations.conditions: Series L-C-R circuit connected to an AC source of angular frequency ω
steps: Write the expression for the impedance of a series L-C-R circuit: Z = √[R<sup>2</sup> + (ωL - 1/(ωC))<sup>2</sup>].
Apply the condition for resonance where the reactive components cancel out: ω<sub>r</sub>L = 1/(ω<sub>r</sub>C).
Rearrange the equation to solve for the resonant angular frequency ω<sub>r</sub>: ω<sub>r</sub><sup>2</sup> = 1/(LC).
Take the square root to find the linear resonant frequency f<sub>r</sub> = ω<sub>r</sub>/(2π).

derivations.title: Derivation of Bandwidth and Q-Factor
derivations.conditions: Half-power frequencies where circuit power drops to half of its maximum value
steps: Set the impedance equal to \sqrt{2}R, which corresponds to the frequencies where current drops to 1/\sqrt{2} of its maximum value.
Identify the two half-power frequencies ω<sub>1</sub> and ω<sub>2</sub> such that ω<sub>2</sub> - ω<sub>1</sub> = R/L.
Define bandwidth BW as the difference between the upper and lower half-power frequencies: BW = R/L.
Define Q-factor as the ratio of resonant frequency to bandwidth: Q = \frac{\omega_r}{BW}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Current vs Frequency Resonance Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of RMS current (I) on the y-axis versus frequency (f) on the x-axis, showing a sharp peak at f<sub>r</sub> for smaller R and a flatter peak for larger R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates that current is maximum at f<sub>r</sub> and decreases symmetrically on both sides. Smaller resistance results in a sharper peak (higher selectivity).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual questions regarding the effect of resistance on the sharpness of resonance.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Impedance vs Frequency Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of impedance (Z) on the y-axis versus frequency (f) on the x-axis, showing a minimum dip at f<sub>r</sub> equal to R, with X<sub>L</sub> increasing linearly and X<sub>C</sub> hyperbolically decreasing.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At frequencies below f<sub>r</sub>, the circuit is capacitive (Z dominated by X<sub>C</sub>); above f<sub>r</sub>, it is inductive (Z dominated by X<sub>L</sub>).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in identifying the nature of the circuit (inductive or capacitive) below and above resonance.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Phase Angle vs Frequency Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of phase angle (φ) versus frequency (f), where φ goes from -90° at low frequencies to 0° at f<sub>r</sub>, and up to +90° at high frequencies.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the transition from a lagging/leading power factor to unity power factor exactly at the resonant frequency.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in PGT problems involving complex AC network phase calculations.

solved_numericals.question: A series L-C-R circuit has an inductance L = 2 H, capacitance C = 32 µF, and resistance R = 10 Ω. Calculate the resonant frequency of the circuit.
solution_steps: Identify the given values: L = 2 H, C = 32 × 10<sup>-6</sup> F, R = 10 Ω.
Use the formula for linear resonant frequency: f<sub>r</sub> = 1 / (2π √[LC]).

solved_numericals.question: An L-C-R series circuit with L = 0.5 H, C = 10 µF, and R = 20 Ω is connected to a 200 V variable frequency AC source. Find the resonant frequency, the maximum current, and the quality factor of the circuit.
solution_steps: Calculate resonant angular frequency: ω<sub>r</sub> = 1 / √[LC] = 1 / √[0.5 × 10 × 10<sup>-6</sup>] = 1 / √[5 × 10<sup>-6</sup>] = 1000 / √5 ≈ 447.2 rad/s.
Calculate maximum current: I<sub>max</sub> = V / R = 200 V / 20 Ω = 10 A.
solved_numericals.answer: Resonant frequency = 447.2 rad/s (or 71.2 Hz), Maximum current = 10 A, Q-factor = 11.18

solved_numericals.question: A series resonant circuit has a resonant frequency of 100 kHz and a bandwidth of 2 kHz. If the resistance of the circuit is 10 Ω, find the values of inductance L and capacitance C.
solution_steps: Given f<sub>r</sub> = 100 × 10<sup>3</sup> Hz, BW = 2 × 10<sup>3</sup> Hz, R = 10 Ω.
Use bandwidth formula for series circuit: BW = R / (2π L).
Use resonant frequency formula f<sub>r</sub> = 1 / (2π √[LC]) to find C.
Rearrange for C: C = 1 / (4 π<sup>2</sup> f<sub>r</sub><sup>2</sup> L) = 1 / (4 × (3.1416)<sup>2</sup> × (10<sup>5</sup>)<sup>2</sup> × 0.796 × 10<sup>-3</sup>) ≈ 3.18 nF.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes linear circuit elements (L, C, and R remain constant and independent of frequency and current amplitude).
Does not account for parasitic resistance in the inductor coil or leakage capacitance in practical capacitors unless explicitly modeled as an added series resistance.

common_misconceptions.wrong: At resonance, the voltage across the inductor and capacitor becomes zero because their reactances cancel out.
common_misconceptions.correct: The net reactance of the combination is zero, but individual voltages across L and C are equal in magnitude and 180 degrees out of phase, often resulting in a high non-zero voltage magnification.
common_misconceptions.why: V<sub>L</sub> = I·X<sub>L</sub> and V<sub>C</sub> = I·X<sub>C</sub> are non-zero; they cancel each other out when added phasorially with total reactive drop, but individual component stress exists.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A series resonant circuit acts as a current rejector.
common_misconceptions.correct: A series resonant circuit acts as a current acceptor (or tuner), allowing maximum current to pass at resonance.
common_misconceptions.why: Since impedance is minimum at resonance, current is maximum, unlike parallel resonance where impedance is maximum and current is minimum.

quick_revision: At series resonance, X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>, Z = R, current is maximum, and the power factor is unity.
